title: I want to play like Adam Jones
goal: Play like Tool guitarist Adam Jones: drop D riffs, odd meters, dissonant voicings and texture instead of solos.

phases.title: Drop D and the Riff Hand

steps.title: Where Jones comes from: Crimson, the Melvins and a sculptor's ear
steps.description:
[Before you start]
This roadmap assumes an intermediate player: power chords and barre chords, palm muting, alternate picking at a moderate tempo, and the ability to keep time with a click in 4/4. You need an electric guitar you can retune to drop D and any amp or simulator with a usable high-gain sound. By the end you will play drop D riffs the way Jones builds them, count and play odd meters and cross rhythms, use dissonance and texture instead of solos, dial a tone close to his, play six Tool songs, and record a piece of your own in odd time.

[What it is]
A listening map and a first playing session. Jones had Suzuki violin lessons and played double bass in an orchestra, never took a guitar lesson, and learned alongside Tom Morello in a school band called Electric Sheep, where Jones played bass. He spent the years before Tool making film effects and sculpture under people like Stan Winston. What he names as influences is a short, specific list: Robert Fripp and King Crimson, the Melvins, Helmet, and later Meshuggah.

[Why it matters]
Everything unusual about his playing follows from that background. A sculptor and a former bass player thinks in shapes, weight and space rather than in licks, which is why Wikipedia's summary of his style is a list of textures: "power chords, scratchy noise, chiming arpeggios, off-beat rhythm patterns, and quiet minimalism". Fripp, he says, taught him the two things that matter most in playing: attitude and discipline. If you come to this roadmap expecting scale runs you will learn the wrong thing.

[How to practice]
Make a listening list and play one track per session before you touch an exercise: King Crimson's "Larks' Tongues in Aspic, Part Two", the Melvins' "Honey Bucket", Helmet's "Unsung", Black Sabbath's "Symptom of the Universe", then Tool's "Stinkfist", "Schism", "Forty Six & 2" and "7empest". For each, write one sentence about what the guitar is doing rhythmically, not melodically. Then tune to drop D (sixth string down a whole step to D) and play the Metal Guitar Playalong with a high-gain sound, locking to the drums rather than chasing the lead.
steps.successCriteria: Your guitar is in drop D and you can play the Metal Guitar Playalong through a high-gain tone locked to the drums. You have written one sentence per track for eight listening examples describing what the guitar does rhythmically, and can name four players or bands Jones has cited and what each contributes to his sound.

lessons.title: Top 10 Tool Adam Jones Guitar Riffs with TABS
Tool Guitar Playing Tricks from Adam Jones for #guitar Riffs!

steps.title: Drop D: one finger, three strings
steps.description:
[What it is]
In drop D the bottom three strings are tuned a fifth and an octave apart, so one finger laid flat across them at any fret gives a full power chord, and the open strings give the D. On top of that: the same barre moved as a shape, the sus2 that appears when you lift a finger, and the fifth on the fourth and third strings for higher voicings.

[Why it matters]
This is the physical fact the whole style rests on. Jones used drop D almost exclusively on Fear Inoculum, and MusicRadar's first lesson on playing like him is that in drop D "powerchords can be played with just one finger barring across the three bass strings". A one-finger chord leaves the other three fingers free to hammer, ornament and mute, which is what the next three steps are about. It also means riffs can move fast across the neck without the hand reshaping.

[How to practice]
Tune to drop D and check the octave: the open sixth string should match the fourth string an octave down. Play Down Picking — Slow & Heavy at 60 BPM, all downstrokes, palm muted, first on the open D, then barring the bottom three strings at the second, fifth, seventh and tenth frets. Keep the barre finger flat and the other fingers hovering, not gripping. Then play the "Stinkfist" main figure: the open bottom three strings against the same shape at the third and second frets. Raise to 80 and 100 BPM only when every chord speaks with no rattle from the barre.
steps.successCriteria: You can play one-finger drop D power chords cleanly at the second, fifth, seventh and tenth frets, move between them in eighth notes at 100 BPM with all downstrokes and palm muting, and play the "Stinkfist" main figure in time with the record.

lessons.title: Beginner Guitar Gold: 1 Finger Drop D Chords!
Expand Your Drop D Power Chords
The Music Theory of POWER CHORDS

steps.title: Palm muting and the muted triplet
steps.description:
[What it is]
The heel of the picking hand resting at the bridge so the low strings chug instead of ring, held steady while the riff moves; and the three-note grouping that the palm-muted hand plays over and over in Tool riffs, where a picked note is followed by two hammer-ons under constant muting.

[Why it matters]
MusicRadar's third lesson on Jones is the palm-muted triplet hammer-on, with "a three-note grouping for a typical Adam Jones-style riff", and names "Schism" and "Vicarious" as where you hear it. The mute is not a special effect here: it is the default state of the picking hand, and the moments when the strings are allowed to ring are the events. If the mute drifts, everything downstream sounds like a different band.

[How to practice]
Set the hand at the bridge so a low D still has pitch but no sustain, and do not move it for the whole exercise. Play Gallop Picking — Thrash Rhythm at 60 BPM for the coordination, counting the triplets aloud. Then the Jones grouping: pick the open D, hammer the second fret with the first finger, hammer the third fret with the second, all palm muted, three notes per beat. Loop for two minutes, checking the mute has not slid towards the neck. Then alternate two bars muted with two bars open on the same figure.
steps.successCriteria: A two-minute recording of the palm-muted triplet grouping at 90 BPM has an even chug with no note ringing out, no drift in the hand position, and every hammer-on as loud as the picked note. You can switch between muted and open bars without the tempo moving.

lessons.title: How to Palm Mute for Rock & Metal | Blackstar Potential Lesson
Mastering Palm Muting On Guitar: A Comprehensive Guide
GALLOPING PALM MUTED RIFFS | Metal Guitar Techniques

steps.title: The lift: hammer-ons with no pick
steps.description:
[What it is]
Jones's signature move, and the reason his riffs sound like two guitars. In drop D you hammer the second fret of the bottom three strings with one flattened finger, no pick at all, so the sound comes only from the force of the fretting hand; then pull off and hammer on again, and pick the open D and G strings for the bright notes on top. The same grip gives a moveable shape: the first finger across the top three strings with the third and fourth fingers on the fourth and fifth strings.

[Why it matters]
It is what makes "Jambi", "Invincible" and the heavier parts of Fear Inoculum sound the way they do, and no amount of picking accuracy substitutes for it. The technique exists because he plays in drop D: the tuning puts a whole chord under one finger, so the fretting hand can produce notes on its own while the picking hand does something else. Learning it converts a picking-hand player into a two-hand riff player.

[How to practice]
Unplug first, or play very quietly, so you can hear how weak the hammer is. Flatten the first finger across the bottom three strings and hammer it onto the second fret hard enough that all three strings sound without any pick. Pull off, hammer again, for a minute. Then add the pick on the open D and G between hammers. Play Legato — Scale Run slowly for the general hammer-and-pull volume. Finally learn the "Jambi" intro figure from the Ben Eller and Maya Neelakantan lessons at half speed, then at tempo.
steps.successCriteria: With the amp off you can make all three bottom strings sound by hammering alone, evenly, ten times in a row. Plugged in, you can loop the hammer-and-pick figure for two minutes at 80 BPM with the hammered notes as loud as the picked ones, and play the "Jambi" intro figure at tempo.

lessons.title: The weird technique Adam Jones uses to play Jambi (Tool)! Weekend Wankshop 193
Jambi (TOOL) Intro - Adam Jones' Unique Technique!

steps.title: Open-string drones under moving shapes
steps.description:
[What it is]
Letting an open string ring while a fretted shape moves against it, so the harmony shifts but the root stays put. In drop D the open D sits under everything; the open G and A do the same job higher up. Together with two- and three-note partial shapes, this is how one guitar covers a whole section.

[Why it matters]
Premier Guitar's lesson on Jones puts it plainly: an "open string creates an almost drone-like quality. That's another signature part of Tool's music." The drone is also what lets the bass carry the harmonic changes while the guitar repeats: guitarguitar describes Jones creating "a lot of space in his sound by using comparatively few notes and plenty of ambience, and by repeating lots of patterns". Getting the drone to ring cleanly under a moving shape is a muting problem, not a fretting one.

[How to practice]
Play Muting — Inside a D Chord to train relaxing single fingers without lifting them, which is exactly the control a drone needs. Then hold the open D ringing and move a two-note shape on the fourth and third strings up the neck in whole steps, listening that the D never chokes. Add the open G as a second drone. Record thirty seconds and check that the drone is continuous, not restruck, and that no unwanted string is sounding.
steps.successCriteria: Over a held open D you can move a two-note shape through four positions with the drone ringing continuously and no unwanted string audible in a recording, and do the same with the open G as the drone.

lessons.title: 3 Easy Drop D Riffs - Cool Guitar Lesson On Heavy Metal Riffs
10 Iconic Drop D Guitar Riffs (with Tabs)

steps.title: Picking dynamics: whisper to wall
steps.description:
[What it is]
Controlling how hard the pick hits, so the same riff can sit almost inaudible under a verse and then arrive at full weight, and so single notes inside a muted passage can be accented without changing the tempo or the mute.

[Why it matters]
Tool songs are built on the distance between quiet and crushing, and under high gain that distance comes from the hand, not the volume knob: a heavily saturated amp compresses, so only a real change in attack reads as a change in dynamics. This is also the discipline behind the quote that ends the next phase, that not playing can be as powerful as playing. A player with one attack level has one texture.

[How to practice]
Play Chromatic — Moving Accents, which asks for clearly louder accented notes and clearly quieter ones in the same line. Then take the palm-muted triplet figure from two steps back and play it four bars as quietly as the amp will still speak, four bars at full force, and four bars moving between the two without a break. Record and check the difference is audible through the distortion.
steps.successCriteria: In a recording of one riff played at three attack levels through a high-gain tone, the three levels are obviously different, the tempo and palm-mute position do not change, and accented notes inside a muted passage stand out without breaking the chug.

lessons.title: How To Control The Dynamics In Your Guitar Playing

steps.title: Counting odd meters: 7/8 and 5/8
steps.description:
[What it is]
Bars that do not divide evenly: seven eighth notes grouped 2+2+3 or 3+2+2, five grouped 3+2 or 2+3. You count the grouping, not the number, and your foot taps the groups rather than every eighth.

[Why it matters]
Odd meter is the first thing anyone notices about Tool, and Jones uses 7/8 throughout the intro of "7empest". Without a counting system you can learn a riff by muscle memory and still get lost the moment the drums do something unexpected, which is the normal state of affairs in this band. Counting groups instead of numbers is what lets an odd bar feel like a groove rather than an arithmetic problem.

[How to practice]
Play Meter — 4/4 ↔ 7/8 at 60 BPM, counting aloud in groups: "one two, one two, one two three". Tap the foot only on the first note of each group. When that is automatic, swap the grouping to 3+2+2 and hear how the riff moves. Then Meter — 3/4 ↔ 5/8 for five, counted "one two three, one two". Play a one-finger drop D power chord on the first note of every group so the meter is audible in what you play, not just in your counting.
steps.successCriteria: You can play the 4/4 to 7/8 and 3/4 to 5/8 exercises at 80 BPM counting aloud in groups without losing the bar, accent the first note of each group, and re-enter correctly after four bars of silence from the click.

lessons.title: Odd Time Signatures • 5/4, 5/8, 7/8
How to Play and Hear Odd Time Signatures (5/4, 7/8, 9/8, 11/8) - Guitar Lesson Tutorial
Count And Play Odd Time Signatures Easily - 7/8 5/4 15/16

steps.title: Riffs that alternate meters: 5/8 plus 7/8
steps.description:
[What it is]
A riff whose bars are not all the same length: one bar of 5/8 followed by one of 7/8, repeating. The pair adds up to twelve eighths, so the cycle feels circular even though neither half is symmetrical. This is the verse of "Schism".

[Why it matters]
It is the most famous rhythmic idea in the band's catalogue and the clearest example of how Jones writes: the riff is built around D, A and F, leaning on fourths and fifths, and the interest comes from the bar lengths rather than from the notes. Learning to hold an alternating pair teaches you to keep a cycle in your head instead of a count, which is the only way these parts stay playable at speed.

[How to practice]
Count the pair aloud with no guitar first: "one two three, one two | one two three, one two, one two three", tapping the group heads. Then play one muted drop D chord on each group head, so the shape of the cycle is in your hands. Use Meter — 3/4 ↔ 5/8 at a slow tempo for the 5/8 half. Then write your own two-bar figure on the cycle: one note per group head first, then fill the groups in. Test yourself by counting the cycle out loud while playing it.
steps.successCriteria: You can loop an alternating 5/8 and 7/8 cycle for three minutes at 80 BPM while counting the groups aloud, and re-enter on the first group head after four bars of silence without losing the cycle.

lessons.title: Odd Time Signatures GUITAR RIFFS | LESSON +TABS | Rock Metal TUTORIAL | 7/8 - 5/4 - 7/4
Feeling Advanced Rhythms | How to Count Odd Time Signatures like 5/4 & 7/4

steps.title: Odd groupings inside 4/4
steps.description:
[What it is]
Staying in 4/4 but grouping the sixteenth notes unevenly, so the riff sounds like it is in odd time while the bar is not: seven, seven and two sixteenths inside a bar, or five eighths repeated three times plus one across a longer cycle. The accents move against the beat until they line up again.

[Why it matters]
Premier Guitar's lesson shows a riff where "each measure can follow a 7-7-2 grouping to give the riff an odd-time feel without actually leaving 4/4", and MusicRadar describes the same device in "Rosetta Stoned" as five eighth notes repeated three times plus one, with bass and drums moving out of sync against it. This is the trick behind riffs that listeners cannot count: the meter is ordinary and the grouping is not.

[How to practice]
Play Meter — 8/8 Regrouped (3+3+2 against 2+3+3) at 60 BPM so the ear learns the same bar length carrying two different groupings. Then, in 4/4 with a click on the quarter note, play a muted sixteenth-note figure accented every seven sixteenths and count where the accent lands in each bar; keep going until the pattern comes back around to beat one. Write down where the accents fall in each of the four bars before you speed up.
steps.successCriteria: Over a 4/4 click at 80 BPM you can play a sixteenth-note riff accented every seven sixteenths for four bars and land back on beat one, and you can say before you play where the accent falls in each bar.

lessons.title: STOP Counting To Seven — THIS Is How Pros Play ODD TIME Signatures [Rhythm Guitar]
Basic Riff Syncopation - Modern Metal Rhythm Guitar, Lesson 5
Rhythm Guitar Mastery & The Power of Syncopation!

steps.title: Cross rhythms: three against four
steps.description:
[What it is]
Two rhythms running at once: your part in threes while the drums are in fours, or the reverse, both lining up only at the start of the cycle. The 6/8 against 3/4 hemiola is the simplest version and the gateway to the rest.

[Why it matters]
Jones's riffs frequently sit against a drum part that is counting something else, and the polyrhythmic, mathematical side of Tool is where the King Crimson influence is most audible. A guitarist who can only hear their own part will drift the moment the drums imply a different grouping. Being able to hold three against four is what makes playing with a drummer like this possible at all.

[How to practice]
Play Meter — 6/8 ↔ 3/4 Hemiola at a slow tempo until the switch feels like a change of feel rather than a change of speed. Then set a click on the quarter note and play triplets grouped in twos, or eighth notes grouped in threes, until the accent pattern resolves. Say the classic counting phrase for three against four out loud while tapping. Finally play a drop D riff in threes over a four-beat click for two minutes without drifting.
steps.successCriteria: Against a quarter-note click at 80 BPM you can play a riff grouped in threes for two minutes and stay locked, switch between 6/8 and 3/4 feels on cue, and land on beat one at the end of each cycle.

lessons.title: POLYRHYTHM- Learn and MASTER 3:4 and 4:3 [MUSIC THEORY - RHYTHM- COUNTING]
4 Against 3 Polyrhythm Made Easy
Polyrhythms for Guitar Lesson Part One 4 over 3 - Garner Guitar

steps.title: Space: the power of not playing
steps.description:
[What it is]
Writing and playing parts with deliberate silence in them: a riff that states itself and stops, long rests where a lesser part would fill, and single sustained chords held while the rest of the band moves. Counting continues through the silence.

[Why it matters]
Jones has described this as the discipline he learned in writing: "You learn that not playing can be just as powerful as playing. You need to let things breathe... That silence just makes the times that I do play have much more impact." It is also a practical consequence of the band's arrangement: with a bass player carrying harmonic movement and a drummer filling the space, a busy guitar makes the arrangement worse. Restraint here is a technique, not a mood.

[How to practice]
Play Phrasing — Two Notes Per Bar over a slow backing track, which forces the constraint. Then take a riff you already have and delete half of it, keeping the count going through the holes; record both versions and compare which sounds heavier. Practise entering after two bars of silence exactly on the downbeat. Do the same over a 7/8 cycle, where re-entry is harder.
steps.successCriteria: You have two recordings of the same riff, full and halved, and the halved version is the one a listener calls heavier. You can re-enter exactly on the downbeat after two bars of silence, in 4/4 and in 7/8.

lessons.title: Top 10 Tool Adam Jones Guitar Riffs

steps.title: Phrygian and Phrygian dominant
steps.description:
[What it is]
Two dark scales built on D, the home note of drop D. D Phrygian is the minor scale with a flattened second, so the half step between D and E flat sits right next to the root. D Phrygian dominant raises the third: D, E flat, F sharp, G, A, B flat, C, which puts an augmented second between E flat and F sharp.

[Why it matters]
Premier Guitar's lesson on riffing like Jones uses exactly these two, noting that in Phrygian dominant "the minor third between Eb and F# gives this scale its distinctive sound". The flattened second is the source of the menace: it is a half step from the root, so every time the riff touches it the tonic is under threat. Because the tuning fixes D as the root, these scales are where drop D riffs naturally live.

[How to practice]
Use Scale Practice — Pick Your Scale set to D Phrygian, one octave on the bottom three strings first, at 60 BPM, saying the flattened second aloud when you hit it. Then write a four-bar riff that starts and ends on D and uses the E flat on a strong beat. Repeat with Phrygian dominant, aiming the F sharp against the E flat so the wide interval is audible. Keep the rhythms simple: the colour, not the speed, is the point.
steps.successCriteria: You can play D Phrygian and D Phrygian dominant on the bottom three strings without hesitation, name the note that makes each dark, and play two four-bar riffs of your own, one per scale, that resolve to D and place the characteristic note on a strong beat.

lessons.title: PHRYGIAN - Understanding and Using the Third Mode of Major [MODAL MUSIC THEORY]
Phrygian for Rock & Metal Guitar
Complex Phrygian Riff - Modern Metal Rhythm Guitar, Lesson 3

steps.title: Fourths, fifths and open intervals
steps.description:
[What it is]
Building riffs from bare fourths and fifths instead of full chords, so the harmony stays ambiguous: no third means no major or minor, and the part sits under a vocal without arguing with it. The "Schism" material is the model, built around D, A and F and leaning on fourths and fifths.

[Why it matters]
Open intervals are why Tool riffs sound huge without sounding like standard metal. They also leave room for the bass to define the harmony, which is exactly how the band divides the work. Knowing fourths and fifths as shapes anywhere on the neck, rather than as one power-chord grip, is what lets a riff move without becoming a chord progression.

[How to practice]
Play Note Hunt — Intervals restricted to perfect fourths and fifths until you find either instantly from any root. Then take three notes (D, A and F) and write a riff that only uses those notes and the intervals between them, moving position rather than adding notes. Try the same three notes as double stops on adjacent strings. Finally play the "Schism" figure and mark which interval each two-note shape is.
steps.successCriteria: You can find a perfect fourth or fifth from any root instantly on the bottom four strings, and you have written a riff using only three note names that changes character by moving position and interval rather than by adding notes.

lessons.title: Learn Fretboard Shapes - Playing the Perfect Fifth on Guitar (Power Chord) Guitar Intervals Lesson
Learn Fretboard Shapes - Perfect 4th Guitar Interval - Music theory applied to guitar

steps.title: Dissonant dyads: the half step and the tritone
steps.description:
[What it is]
Two-note shapes chosen for the clash: a minor second or its inversion held against the drone, a tritone from the root, a ninth rubbing against the octave. Played under gain, on adjacent or skipped strings, and either resolved or deliberately left hanging.

[Why it matters]
Jones's chords are routinely described as unusual and dissonant, often using open strings against fretted notes to get there. Dissonance is how his parts create tension without speeding up or adding notes, which is the whole economy of his style. Two notes also cut through a dense mix in a way that a six-string chord under distortion cannot.

[How to practice]
Use Chords — Degree Hunt (Tensions) to learn where the ninths, elevenths and thirteenths sit around a chord, because those are the notes that supply the clash. Then hold the open D drone and find, one at a time, the E flat, the A flat and the ninth above it on the fourth and third strings; play each as a dyad against the drone for a full bar and decide whether it should resolve. Build a four-bar part where one dyad resolves and one does not.
steps.successCriteria: Over an open D drone you can play at least four dissonant dyads on demand, name the interval in each, and perform a four-bar part where one clash resolves and one is deliberately left hanging, with both sounding intentional in a recording.

lessons.title: Periphery's Mark Holcomb - How to Build Dissonant, Jarring Chords
How to Use the 3 Most Dissonant Intervals
Black Metal Lesson #21 - Building Evil, Dissonant Chords

steps.title: Clusters, sliding shapes and open-string voicings
steps.description:
[What it is]
Close three-note voicings that sit on adjacent strings, chords that keep one or two fingers in place while the rest move, and shapes slid bodily up or down the neck with the open strings still ringing so the harmony changes underneath a constant drone.

[Why it matters]
This is how Jones gets chord movement without ever sounding like a chord progression: a shape slides, the open strings stay, and the relationship between them changes from consonant to sour and back. Sliding a shape also keeps the fretting hand economical, which matters when the same hand has to hammer and mute in the same bar.

[How to practice]
Play Chords — Smooth Changes with a fixed three-string set and minimal finger motion, which trains exactly the grip control this needs. Then take a three-note shape on the fourth, third and second strings and slide it through four positions over a ringing open D and G, stopping at each to decide whether it sounds resolved. Try both a legato slide, picked once, and a re-picked arrival. Record four bars of each.
steps.successCriteria: You can slide one three-string shape through four positions over ringing open strings with the drone unbroken, play the move both as a single-picked legato slide and as a re-picked arrival, and say which positions sound resolved and which do not.

lessons.title: Open String Chords - Open String Voicings

steps.title: Chiming arpeggios and clean figures
steps.description:
[What it is]
The quiet side of the catalogue: sustained arpeggiated figures on a clean or barely broken-up tone, picked one note at a time with the notes left to ring into each other, usually over a drone and usually repeating with small changes.

[Why it matters]
Premier Guitar describes Tool's music as shifting between heavy power-chord sequences and "sustained arpeggiated figures that form subdued, melodic motifs", and Wikipedia's style summary lists chiming arpeggios alongside the power chords. These sections are not filler: they are what makes the heavy sections land, and they are where the dynamic range of a Tool song comes from.

[How to practice]
Play Mini Arpeggio slowly, letting every note ring rather than stopping it. Then take a three-note shape from the previous step and arpeggiate it over an open drone in a repeating eighth-note pattern, changing one note every four bars. Keep the picking hand light and consistent, close to the neck for a rounder sound. Record two minutes and listen for notes choking because a finger lifted early.
steps.successCriteria: You can play a repeating arpeggiated figure over a drone for two minutes with every note ringing into the next, no choked notes in the recording, and a single note changed every four bars that a listener can hear as a development rather than a mistake.

lessons.title: 3 Exercises to MASTER guitar ARPEGGIOS

steps.title: Long notes: sustain, vibrato and the held bend
steps.description:
[What it is]
Holding one note for a whole bar or more and making it interesting: an even, wide vibrato driven from the wrist and forearm, a bend taken slowly to pitch and held, and the decision to start the vibrato late rather than immediately.

[Why it matters]
When a guitarist plays as few notes as Jones does, the ones that remain have to carry the weight, and a long note with no vibrato under high gain sounds like a mistake. This is the substitute for a solo: the lead statements in his playing are usually one sustained note placed exactly where the arrangement opens up. It also sets up the feedback work in the next step, which needs a note that is already ringing steadily.

[How to practice]
Play Vibrato — Hold a Whole Bar with its backing track, switching the vibrato on and off at exact beats. Then hold a note for four bars: one bar plain, three with a slow wide vibrato, checking the pitch centre does not creep upward. Then bend a whole step over two beats, hold the top for two bars with vibrato, and release over a beat. Record and listen for the pitch wobbling below the target.
steps.successCriteria: A recorded four-bar held note has an even vibrato at a chosen width and speed with a stable pitch centre, a delayed start, and a whole-step bend held for two bars that stays in tune before a controlled release.

lessons.title: Make YOUR Vibrato sound awesome (Guitar Lesson)

steps.title: Controlled feedback
steps.description:
[What it is]
Making the guitar and amp sing together on purpose: finding the spot in the room where a fretted note blooms into a harmonic instead of dying, holding it there, and stopping it cleanly when the part needs silence. And the opposite skill, keeping everything else quiet while one note rings.

[Why it matters]
Feedback is an instrument in this style rather than an accident, used to extend a note past the point where the string would stop and to add a harmonic that nobody played. Because the tone is saturated, the difference between a controlled bloom and a squeal is entirely in the muting and the body position. Jones's own description of his stage presence as a shoegazer thing is partly this: standing still, working the amp.

[How to practice]
Play Muting — One Note at a Time first, so everything except the target note is dead; feedback control is mostly muting control. Then, at a volume that is loud but safe, hold a note at the twelfth fret and move slowly towards and across the speaker until the note blooms. Mark where you stood. Practise starting the bloom on a chosen beat and killing it on another. If you cannot play loud, use the no-amp feedback method in the Shadow lesson or a sustain-heavy plugin for the timing half of the skill.
steps.successCriteria: You can make a fretted note bloom into feedback within two seconds from a repeatable position, start it on a chosen beat and stop it on another, and in a recording nothing except the target note is audible before the bloom.

lessons.title: How To Get Infinite Sustain With Controlled Amp Feedback | Guitar Tutorial | Quick Tips
Guitar Feedback: How to Do It / How to Use It
How to Use & Control Guitar Feedback - Guitar Lesson / Tutorial
How To Make Guitar Feedback WITHOUT An Amp (Easy to Follow Guide)

steps.title: Volume swells and fade-ins
steps.description:
[What it is]
Striking a chord or note with the guitar's volume rolled off and raising it afterwards, so there is no attack at all and the sound appears out of nothing. Done with the little finger on the volume knob or with a volume pedal, usually into delay or reverb so the swell has somewhere to go.

[Why it matters]
MusicRadar lists ambient volume swells as one of five ways to play like Jones, pointing at the atmosphere of Fear Inoculum, and suggests pairing them with a delay set to a dotted eighth. The swell is how a guitar enters a Tool arrangement without announcing itself, and it is the clean counterpart to the feedback work: both are ways of sustaining sound whose beginning and end you control.

[How to practice]
Play Clean Tone — Slow Melody with the volume rolled down before each note and swelled in, so the discipline is attached to something musical. Set the knob to zero, strike a chord, and raise the volume over two beats; then over one beat; then over four. Aim for no audible pick attack at any speed. Add a delay and practise timing the swell so the repeat arrives as the swell peaks. Finally swell into a chord change so the new chord appears while the old one is still fading.
steps.successCriteria: In a recording, ten consecutive swells have no audible pick attack, at three different swell lengths on request, and you can swell into a chord change with a delay so the repeat arrives as the swell reaches full volume.

Ambient Guitar Swells Tutorial: Techniques & Settings

steps.title: Noise as a part: scrapes, scratches and dead notes
steps.description:
[What it is]
Sounds with no pitch used as rhythm: the pick dragged along a wound string, muted strings struck for a percussive click, dead notes filling the gaps between fretted ones, and the deliberate scratch that opens or closes a section.

[Why it matters]
Wikipedia's summary of his technique lists "scratchy noise" and pick slides next to the power chords, and guitarguitar describes his focus as "textures, not notes", including unconventional picking to change timbre: he famously used an epilator as a plectrum on Ænima and Lateralus. Treating noise as material rather than as a mistake is a large part of why a Tool guitar track sounds like a machine rather than a guitarist.

[How to practice]
Play Rhythm Training — Medium, which is performed on a muted string, so the whole exercise is dead-note timing. Then place a pick scrape on the last beat of a four-bar riff, in the same spot each time, and record until the scrape sounds deliberate. Fill the silent sixteenths of a palm-muted riff with dead notes so the chug is continuous. Try two different picks and a coin on the same riff and record the difference.
steps.successCriteria: A four-bar riff recorded with a pick scrape in a fixed position sounds intentional on every repeat, the silent subdivisions are filled with dead notes that keep the chug continuous, and you can demonstrate two clearly different timbres from two picking objects.

lessons.title: Guitar String Muting Techniques - How To Play Guitar - Stage 3 Guitar Lesson [IM-134]

steps.title: Single-note melodies over a drone
steps.description:
[What it is]
The haunting single-note line that sits on top of a Tool riff: slow, mostly stepwise, drawn from the dark scales of the previous phase, placed over a static drone or a repeating figure, and repeated with small changes rather than developed into a solo.

[Why it matters]
Guitar World describes Jones as fusing "monstrous powerchords, haunting single-note melodies and off-kilter time signatures", and this is the melodic half of that. It is also where his refusal to solo becomes a positive technique: he told Guitar World in 2006 "I was always bored with three-hour solos" and that a solo is fine "if it's tasteful and it's what the song needs". A repeated melodic cell that grows across a section does the work a solo would do, without the display.

[How to practice]
Play Improv — One Chord over a static backing, restricting yourself to D Phrygian and to no more than six notes per phrase. Record four minutes and then throw away everything except the best four-bar idea. Play that idea over the drone for a full minute, changing exactly one thing each time it returns: its register, its rhythm, its last note. Add vibrato and a swell from the earlier steps to the longest note in it.
steps.successCriteria: You have one four-bar melodic idea in D Phrygian that you can play over a drone for a minute, changing a single element on each return, with vibrato and a swell on its longest note and no phrase longer than six notes.

lessons.title: Guitar Practice: Adam Jones Instagram Riff (Sample From Tool's Descending)

steps.title: The rig: a Silverburst into three amps
steps.description:
[What it is]
What Jones actually plays through, and how to approximate it. A 1979 Gibson Les Paul Custom in Silverburst, reissued as his signature model in 2020. Three amplifiers running at once and blended: a hot-rodded mid-1970s Marshall Super Bass with both channels wired together into a Mesa 2x15 bass cabinet, and two Diezel VH4 heads into Mesa 4x12 cabinets. In the studio the list widens: a Sunn Beta Lead on Lateralus, a Roland JC-120 on 10,000 Days.

[Why it matters]
The reason his tone is unmistakable is not one amp but the blend: a bass amp supplying the low weight, a high-gain head supplying the saturation, and a clean or odd third voice on top. Any player can approximate that with three amp channels or three simulator instances panned and blended, and doing so teaches more about his sound than chasing a single pedal. It also explains why his gain never turns to mush: each amp handles one part of the spectrum.

[How to practice]
Play Tone — Match the Reference to train the comparison habit. Then build three tones separately: a thick low-end tone with almost no treble, a saturated mid-forward tone, and a clean tone with high headroom. Blend them, starting with the saturated one at the front and the bass amp underneath. Record the "Stinkfist" figure through each alone and through the blend, and compare with the record. Write down the settings in plain words so they can be rebuilt on other gear.
steps.successCriteria: You have three saved tones (low weight, saturated mids, clean headroom) and one blend of them, and a recording of the same riff through each alone and through the blend where the blend is the one that sits closest to the record.

Getting 'THE' Adam Jones Guitar Tone
Recreating The Adam Jones TOOL Guitar Tone!

steps.title: Pickup and EQ: bridge humbucker, mids forward
steps.description:
[What it is]
The front end of the tone. Jones plays a Les Paul Custom with a hot bridge humbucker, a Seymour Duncan in the bridge position, and the sound is built on mids rather than scooped away from them. The EQ job is to keep the low end tight enough that drop D chords stay defined, and to leave enough upper mid that a single note reads over the band.

[Why it matters]
Drop D plus heavy gain plus a scooped EQ is how most players lose definition, and it is the opposite of what this rig does. A mid-forward bridge humbucker into a bass-heavy amp blend is what keeps a one-finger power chord from turning into a wall of mud. Getting this right makes every earlier technique audible; getting it wrong makes the muting and hammer work inaudible no matter how well you play it.

[How to practice]
Play Tone — Pick Position & Angle to hear how much of the tone is in your hands before touching a knob. Then cycle the pickup selector on the same drop D riff and pick the position where the low string stays defined. Set the amp with mids up rather than down and roll the bass back until the low D stops flapping. A/B against a Tool track at the same volume and adjust one control at a time. Note the settings in words.
steps.successCriteria: On your rig you can state which pickup and EQ settings you use and why, and in a recording a drop D power chord keeps its definition and a single note cuts through the same tone without a boost.

steps.title: Delay as a compositional voice
steps.description:
[What it is]
Using delay so the repeats become part of the part: a dotted-eighth repeat that turns a simple figure into an interlocking pattern, different delay times panned left and right so one played line becomes two, and trails started and stopped on cue.

[Why it matters]
Premier Guitar's Tool lesson has an example using "different delays on the left and right channel, plus a phaser on one side and a flanger on the other", and MusicRadar suggests a dotted-eighth panning delay for the Fear Inoculum atmosphere. Jones's rig has carried a Line 6 DL4 and Boss DD-3 and DD-5 delays for years. When the guitar plays few notes, the delay does the arranging.

[How to practice]
Set a dotted-eighth delay to the tempo of a riff you already play and listen to where the repeats fall relative to your notes; then simplify the part until the repeats fill the gaps instead of colliding. Play Phrasing — Call & Response so you practise leaving a hole for an answer, which is exactly what the delay fills. Then set two different delay times panned apart and play a single-note line, checking that the result is rhythmically legible rather than a wash.
steps.successCriteria: With a dotted-eighth delay matched to the tempo you can play a figure whose repeats fill its gaps rather than clash, and with two panned delay times a single-note line reads as an interlocking pattern rather than a wash in a recording.

lessons.title: How To Play Dotted 8th Delays: Settings and Exercises
How To Setup Dotted Eighth Delays on Any Delay Pedal (4 ways)

steps.title: Flanger, wah and the talk box
steps.description:
[What it is]
The rest of the pedalboard and what each thing is for. A Boss BF-2 flanger for the metallic sweep on sustained parts, a Dunlop Cry Baby used slowly as a filter rather than as a rhythmic effect, a DOD FX40B equaliser and an MXR Micro Amp to push the front end, a Dyna Comp for the clean parts, and the Heil talk box, run through a Roland JC-120 with a compressor, that plays the solo in "Jambi".

[Why it matters]
These are not decorations: the talk box solo in "Jambi" is one of the few lead statements in the catalogue, and the flanger and wah are how a held chord changes over eight bars without anyone playing a new note. Knowing what each pedal is doing lets you get the same effects from whatever you own, and stops you buying the wrong thing.

[How to practice]
Take one sustained dissonant chord from phase three and hold it for eight bars while sweeping the wah slowly across it, then while a flanger sweeps, then with both off, and record all three. If you have a talk box, learn the "Jambi" solo shape; if not, watch the Fox Gonzo Humbert footage of Jones playing it live and write out what the mouth is doing to the pitch, because the phrasing is vocal and worth understanding either way. Decide for each effect which song section it belongs in.
steps.successCriteria: You have a recording of one sustained chord treated three ways (slow wah, flanger, dry) where each is clearly a different part rather than the same part with an effect on, and you can say which Tool song section each treatment would belong to.

lessons.title: Tool Adam Jones Pedal Settings Explained 2022
Tool "Jambi" - Adam Jones on TalkBox

steps.title: Silence under high gain
steps.description:
[What it is]
Keeping everything quiet that is not supposed to sound: the picking-hand palm covering the strings below the one being played, the fretting-hand fingers laid lightly across the strings above, and both hands killing the sound on rests so a gap is actually a gap.

[Why it matters]
This roadmap is full of parts where silence is the material: the space step, the dead-note step, the stops in the song riffs. Under a saturated tone, an undamped open string turns a rest into a hum and a stop into a decay, which destroys the rhythmic precision that everything else has been building. It is also the prerequisite for controlled feedback, where exactly one note is allowed to ring.

[How to practice]
Play Muting — Both Hands, which sets the two-hand system explicitly. Then take any riff from phase one and play it with the gain higher than you would normally use, recording it; listen back for hum in the rests and for strings ringing under the chug. Fix one source at a time. Finally play four bars of riff followed by four bars of total silence with the amp still loud, and check the silence is really silent.
steps.successCriteria: At a gain setting higher than your usual, a recording of a riff followed by four bars of rest has no audible hum, no ringing string in the rests, and every stop lands exactly on the beat it is written on.

lessons.title: 3 Ways to Eliminate String Noise and Play Tighter Metal Guitar Riffs
Heavy Metal Muting Strings Guitar Lesson

steps.title: Stinkfist and Ænema: the drop D riff in a song
steps.description:
[What it is]
Two songs from Ænima (1996) that put the first phase into practice. "Stinkfist" is the clearest example of one-finger drop D power chords carrying a whole song; "Ænema" adds the hammer slap, where you hammer onto the second fret of the bottom three strings with the fretting hand and use the pick only for the upper notes.

[Why it matters]
These are the songs where his method is easiest to hear because the parts are not hidden by complexity: the tuning, the mute, the hammer and the space are all exposed. They are also the standard entry point for anyone learning Tool, which means there are accurate lessons available and a clear reference recording to check yourself against.

[How to practice]
"Stinkfist" first: learn the main figure, then the verse, then the build, using the Rockin Tabs or Mike Gross lesson. Play it with the record at full speed and count the bars so you never lose the form. Then "Ænema": learn the hammer slap on its own before the song, from the Ben Eller lesson, then the main riff. Record both songs start to finish and mark every place where your mute or your timing slipped.
steps.successCriteria: You can play "Stinkfist" from start to finish with the recording without stopping, and the main riff of "Ænema" with the hammer slap producing all three strings, in one take each, with the mute steady throughout.

steps.title: Schism: 5/8 plus 7/8
steps.description:
[What it is]
The song built on alternating bars of 5/8 and 7/8 that add up to twelve eighths, with a guitar part built around D, A and F that leans on fourths and fifths, and a middle section that changes meter repeatedly. The guitar and the bass interlock rather than double each other.

[Why it matters]
It is the song most people mean when they talk about Tool and odd time, and it is the exam for phase two: if the alternating cycle from that phase is solid, this song is playable; if it is not, no amount of note accuracy will keep you in place. Playing it also teaches the band's division of labour, because the bass carries the main hook while the guitar answers it.

[How to practice]
Count the cycle aloud with the record before playing a note. Learn the verse figure from the Marty Music lesson at half speed, counting groups rather than beats, then the chorus, then the middle section from the GuitarLessons365 lesson. Play along with the record with your part alone in the room and the record quiet, so you can hear whether you are drifting. Finish by playing it with the count spoken out loud over the top.
steps.successCriteria: You can play the verse and chorus of "Schism" with the recording without losing the cycle, re-enter correctly after the middle section, and count the 5/8 and 7/8 groups aloud while playing the verse.

steps.title: Forty Six & 2: pull-offs, 7/8 and the build
steps.description:
[What it is]
A drop D song in which the guitar alternates 4/4 with 7/8, uses pull-offs to the open root string before moving into power chords, and builds from a nearly empty verse to a full ending. Technically undemanding, rhythmically hard.

[Why it matters]
MusicRadar uses this song as its example of alternating time signatures, and the lesson writer at Guitar Lessons 365 notes that although it "contains numerous rhythmic challenges", it is not difficult from a technique standpoint. That combination is the whole point: this is where you find out whether phase two worked. The long build is also a lesson in arrangement, since the same material carries the song by changing density rather than notes.

[How to practice]
Learn the riffs in the order they occur in the song, using the Fearskill or GuitarLessons365 lesson, and write the bar counts of each section on one page before playing along. Practise the 4/4 to 7/8 change on its own until you stop clipping the short bar. Then play the whole song with the record. Finally play it with only a drum track so nothing is holding your place but your own count.
steps.successCriteria: You can play "Forty Six & 2" with the recording from start to finish without stopping, the 4/4 to 7/8 changes land without a clipped bar, and you can play the same form with a drum track only.

steps.title: Lateralus: 9/8 and the long build
steps.description:
[What it is]
The title track of the 2001 album: drop D, a repeating figure in 9/8 with shifting groupings, sections that change meter, and a nine-minute arc that goes from a quiet arpeggiated opening to a full ending without ever becoming a different song.

[Why it matters]
It is the clearest demonstration of the band's structural thinking, and for a guitarist it combines everything so far: a clean chiming figure, a drone, odd meter, dynamics that move by section, and a part that repeats with small changes for minutes at a time. Playing it end to end is an endurance and concentration test as much as a technical one.

[How to practice]
Learn the intro figure clean, with the notes ringing into each other, from the LearnE lesson, and get it steady before adding anything. Count the 9/8 in groups rather than to nine. Build the song section by section, writing the bar count for each, then play the whole thing with the record. Use the Thomann tone video to set a clean and a heavy sound and practise switching between them at the section boundaries.
steps.successCriteria: You can play "Lateralus" with the recording from the intro to the end without stopping, counting the 9/8 in groups, with the clean intro figure ringing cleanly and a deliberate tone or dynamic change at every section boundary.

steps.title: Parabola: other tunings and one real solo
steps.description:
[What it is]
One of the songs Jones did not write in drop D: "Parabol" and "Parabola" use a lower tuning, which many players reach either by retuning down or by using a seven-string. It also contains one of his few conventional lead passages, and a dynamic shape that goes from an almost silent opening to the heaviest riff on the album.

[Why it matters]
It shows that the style is not a trick of one tuning: the same habits, drones, sparse melodies, sudden weight, survive a change of pitch. The solo is worth learning precisely because there are so few of them, and because it is built from held bends and vibrato rather than from runs, which is the argument phase four was making. His use of a Les Paul Classic in ebony on these tracks is also a reminder that the Silverburst is not the only guitar on the records.

[How to practice]
Retune or use a seven-string as the Axe of Creation lesson suggests, and check the intonation before you start. Learn "Parabol" first, quiet and clean, then the transition into "Parabola". Learn the solo from the Jimi Wolf transcription slowly, treating every bend as a pitch target from phase four. Play the pair end to end with the record and record yourself once.
steps.successCriteria: You can play "Parabol" into "Parabola" with the recording in the correct tuning without stopping, with the dynamic jump between them intact, and play the solo with every bend landing on pitch.

lessons.title: Tool Parabola Guitar Tutorial
Tool Parabol & Parabola Guitar Lesson

steps.title: Vicarious, Jambi and 7empest: the later style
steps.description:
[What it is]
Three songs from 10,000 Days (2006) and Fear Inoculum (2019) that show what the style became. "Vicarious" is palm-muted triplet hammer-ons at length; "Jambi" is the pull-through lift plus the talk box solo; "7empest" runs 7/8 through its intro and is the closest thing in the catalogue to a guitar showcase.

[Why it matters]
These parts are the reason the earlier phases exist: the triplet grouping, the lift, the drone, odd meter and the tone are all used at once and at full speed. Fear Inoculum is also almost entirely in drop D, so a single tuning covers all three. Finishing them means the technical half of the roadmap is done and only the writing is left.

[How to practice]
Take one song per fortnight. "Vicarious" from the Fearskill lesson, starting with the triplet figure alone at half speed. "Jambi" from the Axe of Creation lessons, with the lift drilled separately first. "7empest" in sections, counting the 7/8 intro in groups. For each, play with the record, then with drums only, then record yourself and compare with the reference for mute consistency and timing.
steps.successCriteria: You can play the main riffs of all three songs at full speed with the recordings, the "Vicarious" triplet figure for two minutes without the mute drifting, the "Jambi" lift cleanly, and the "7empest" intro counted in groups of 7/8.

steps.title: Riff development: from a seed to a part
steps.description:
[What it is]
Taking a fragment of two or three notes and turning it into a part that can carry a section: deciding where it starts and ends, what repeats, what changes on each repetition, and when to stop adding. Variation by displacement, register, articulation and density rather than by new material.

[Why it matters]
Jones's parts are economical motifs that grow through arrangement rather than through new notes, which is why a Tool riff can hold a listener for four minutes. The skill being trained is knowing when a riff is finished rather than merely longer, which is the opposite of the instinct most players have when writing under a heavy tone.

[How to practice]
Play Composition — Short Phrases for the discipline of a fixed frame. Then take three notes from the D Phrygian work, write a one-bar figure, and produce five variations that change exactly one thing each: the rhythm, the register, the articulation, the last note, the density. Loop each over a drum track for a minute and keep the two that survive. Write down which change made the difference.
steps.successCriteria: From one three-note seed you have five one-bar variations that each change exactly one element, you can name the element in each, and two of them survive a minute-long loop over drums without becoming boring.

steps.title: Writing in odd meters
steps.description:
[What it is]
Composing a riff that lives in an uneven cycle rather than forcing an even riff into one: choosing the grouping first, writing a figure whose accents agree with it, and deciding whether the phrase resolves inside the cycle or across it.

[Why it matters]
Odd meter written badly sounds like a mistake, and written well sounds inevitable. The difference is whether the riff's own accents agree with the grouping. This is where the counting work of phase two becomes creative rather than reproductive, and it is the skill that separates writing in the style from playing someone else's parts in it.

[How to practice]
Play Meter — 5/4 ↔ 7/4 to have both cycles in your hands. Then choose 7/8 grouped 2+2+3, write a one-bar drop D figure whose loudest note falls on each group head, and loop it for two minutes. Then write a second figure that deliberately crosses the barline so it resolves every two bars instead of every one. Record both over a click and check that a listener can find beat one.
steps.successCriteria: You have two riffs of your own in 7/8, one resolving every bar and one every two bars, each loopable for two minutes over a click, with accents that agree with the grouping and a beat one a listener can find.

Odd Time Signatures GUITAR RIFFS | LESSON +TABS | Rock Metal TUTORIAL | 7/8 - 5/4 - 7/4

steps.title: Arrangement: quiet, then crushing
steps.description:
[What it is]
Shaping a piece by density and volume rather than by adding parts: the same figure played clean and arpeggiated, then palm muted, then full; sections that drop to a single drone; and a build that takes minutes rather than bars. Tension created by withholding the heavy version, then released by playing it.

[Why it matters]
This is the structural signature of the band and the reason their heavy sections land. It also depends on everything in phase four: the swells, the sustain and the space are the tools that make a quiet section hold attention. Jones's own summary of the discipline is that silence makes the times he does play have much more impact.

[How to practice]
Play Dynamics — Soft to Loud for the physical control. Then take one riff you wrote and make three versions: clean and arpeggiated, palm muted at half volume, and full. Arrange them into a four-minute plan on paper with bar counts, including one section that is only a drone. Record the whole plan in one take and listen for whether the arrival of the heavy version feels earned or early.
steps.successCriteria: You have a four-minute recorded arrangement of one riff in three densities, including a drone-only section, played in a single take, where the heaviest version does not appear until at least halfway through and a listener calls its arrival earned.

lessons.title: How To Control The Dynamics In Your Guitar Playing

steps.title: Layering and doubling
steps.description:
[What it is]
Recording a part more than once so it thickens, and writing a second part that is not the same as the first: a drone under a moving figure, a clean arpeggio under a muted riff, or a line an octave up that enters only in the last repeat. Each layer has to be playable and useful on its own.

[Why it matters]
A single guitar in a three-piece has to sound like more than one, and doubling is how the records get their weight without a second guitarist. The risk is mush: two layers that play the same rhythm in the same register cancel each other under gain. Writing layers that occupy different registers and rhythms is the arranging skill that makes the earlier texture work audible.

[How to practice]
Play Hybrid Picking — Bass + Chords to train holding two independent voices at once, which is what a layered part has to imply even when played live. Then record a riff twice and listen for whether the double sounds wider or just louder; adjust your timing until it tightens. Then write a second part in a different register that enters only in the second half, and mute each layer in turn to check both still make sense alone.
steps.successCriteria: You have a two-layer recording where each layer works alone, the layers occupy different registers or rhythms, and muting either one leaves something musical; the doubled part sounds wider rather than merely louder.

lessons.title: Double-Tracking Guitars - a Tutorial for Awesome Metal Rhythms
Double Tracking Done Wrong vs Done RIGHT | The Difference

steps.title: Locking with bass and drums
steps.description:
[What it is]
Playing your part as one voice in a three-piece: leaving the harmonic movement to the bass, placing your accents with or deliberately against the drums, holding a cycle while the drums play across it, and knowing where beat one is when nobody is stating it.

[Why it matters]
In Tool the bass frequently carries the hook and the drums count something other than the guitar, which is why guitarguitar describes Jones as leaving the harmonic changes to the bass while he repeats patterns. A guitarist who needs the drums to confirm the beat cannot play this music. This is the practical end of the polyrhythm work in phase two.

[How to practice]
Play Timing — Switch Subdivisions to keep the pocket while the density changes. Then loop one of your odd-meter riffs against a drum track that implies a different grouping, and hold your cycle for three minutes. Practise entering after a drum fill that obscures the downbeat. If you have a band or a bass player, play the riff with the bass taking the melodic movement while you hold the drone, then swap.
steps.successCriteria: Over a drum track implying a different grouping you can hold your own odd-meter cycle for three minutes without drifting, and you can re-enter correctly on the downbeat after a fill that hides it.

lessons.title: STOP Counting To Seven — THIS Is How Pros Play ODD TIME Signatures [Rhythm Guitar]

steps.title: Final: your own piece, in odd time, recorded
steps.description:
[What it is]
One piece of your own, three to five minutes, in an odd meter or with an alternating cycle, built from your own riffs, arranged from quiet to heavy, layered at least twice, using drone, dissonance and one texture from phase four, played on your version of the tone, recorded in one take per layer.

[Why it matters]
Everything before this was learning someone else's vocabulary. This is the test of whether it has become yours: whether you can write a part that is economical rather than empty, odd rather than awkward, and heavy because of its arrangement rather than its gain setting. A recording is also the only honest judge of the mute, the timing and the space.

[How to practice]
Write the plan first on one page: meter, sections, bar counts, which riff appears where, which texture enters when, and where the heaviest version arrives. Record a drum track or program one. Track the main guitar, then the double, then the texture layer. Listen once for timing, once for muting, once for whether anything is there that could be removed, and remove it. Then record the final take.

[What you can do now]
You play drop D riffs with one-finger chords, the hammer-on lift, open drones and a steady mute; you can count and play 7/8, 5/8, alternating cycles, odd groupings inside 4/4 and three against four; you write with Phrygian colour, dissonant dyads and sliding clusters; you use sustain, feedback, swells and noise instead of solos; you can build his tone from three blended voices; you can play six Tool songs; and you have written and recorded a piece of your own in his language.
steps.successCriteria: You have a recorded piece of your own, three to five minutes, in odd meter or an alternating cycle, with at least two guitar layers, a quiet-to-heavy arrangement, a drone, one dissonant voicing and one texture from phase four, played on your own version of his tone.
